people.name: Dorothy Page
people.role: President of the Wasilla-Knik Centennial Committee who planned the celebration for Alaska's 100th anniversary and helped organize the first Iditarod Race

people.name: Lee Ellexson
people.role: Mail carrier who introduced Joe Redington to the Iditarod Trail and the sport of dog mushing in 1948

people.name: Susan Butcher
people.role: Champion musher who won four Iditarod victories with the help of her lead dog Granite; survived a moose attack that killed two of her dogs

people.name: Rick Swenson
people.role: Five-time Iditarod champion whose main leader dog Andy helped him win his first four victories

people.name: Libby Riddles
people.role: Winner of the 1985 Iditarod Race who became a legend after surviving a harrowing night on Norton Bay sea ice; led by dogs Axle and Dugan

people.name: Emmitt Peters
people.role: Winner of the 1975 Iditarod Race from the town of Ruby, nicknamed 'The Yukon Fox'

people.name: Herbie Nayokpuk
people.role: Inupiat musher and ivory carver from Shishmaref who drove into a fierce 1982 storm but was forced to retreat

people.name: Dick Mackey
people.role: Winner of the 1978 Iditarod Race, separated from second place by only the tick of a clock

places.name: Wasilla-Knik
places.significance: Area where Dorothy Page served as president of the Centennial Committee and helped organize the first Iditarod celebration

places.name: Anchorage
places.significance: Starting location for the ceremonial 11-mile start of the modern Iditarod Race

places.name: Willow
places.significance: Actual starting point of the competitive Iditarod Race after the ceremonial start in Anchorage

places.name: Dalzell Gorge
places.significance: Treacherous steep descent from Rainy Pass Lodge, considered a 'controlled fall' where dogs slip and have difficulty getting traction

places.name: Farewell Burn
places.significance: Area scarred by a 1976 fire between Rohn and Nikolai, filled with burned timber, stumps, and tussocks that mushers must navigate around

places.name: McGrath
places.significance: Popular checkpoint village with population of 346, named after US Marshal Peter McGrath, featuring two stores, restaurant, bar, and large airfield

places.name: Shaktoolik
places.significance: Checkpoint where Herbie Nayokpuk and Libby Riddles made memorable decisions to drive into fierce storms

places.name: Norton Bay
places.significance: Sea ice area where Libby Riddles survived a harrowing night in 1985 to win the race and become a legend

dates.event: Joe Redington met Lee Ellexson who introduced him to the Iditarod Trail and dog mushing
First Iditarod Race held as part of Alaska's Centennial celebration
Joe Redington Sr. promised there would be a long-distance race to Nome by 1973 with $50,000 prize money
First long-distance Iditarod Trail Sled Dog Race to Nome was held
Pre-race veterinarian check-ups of all race dogs were implemented
Corporate sponsor pledged $50,000 prize money and rule changes about dog care were made; Emmitt Peters won the race
Iditarod Trail Committee considered postponing the race for two years after sponsorship was withdrawn; fire created the Farewell Burn area
Herbie Nayokpuk drove into a fierce storm at Shaktoolik but was forced to retreat
Libby Riddles won the race after surviving a harrowing night on Norton Bay sea ice, creating the 'Legend of Libby'
Dick Mackey and Rick Swenson were separated by only the tick of a clock for first and second place

trueFalse.statement: Snow machines and snowmobiles pushed dog sledding towards extinction in the mid-1960s.
trueFalse.correction: This new invention threatened the traditional practice of dog sledding in Alaska.

trueFalse.statement: Joe Redington owned 40 dogs after his first winter living in Alaska.
trueFalse.correction: This showed his quick commitment to the sport of dog mushing.

trueFalse.statement: All Iditarod mushers are professional mushers who earn their living from the sport.
trueFalse.correction: Only a handful are professional mushers; most are part-time or hobby mushers with other occupations.

trueFalse.statement: The prize purse has grown to over $500,000 since the 1970s.
trueFalse.correction: The race has steadily grown in prestige and prize money since its early years.

trueFalse.statement: Mushers receive too much credit for wins while dogs labor in obscurity and anonymity.
trueFalse.correction: With few exceptions, the dogs are the unsung heroes who don't receive recognition for their critical role.

trueFalse.statement: Siberian huskies were larger than Malamutes and other mixed-breed huskies.
trueFalse.correction: Siberian huskies were smaller and lighter but had more stamina and speed for long distances.

trueFalse.statement: Pre-race veterinarian check-ups of all race dogs were implemented in 1974.
trueFalse.correction: This was an important safety measure to protect the health of racing dogs.

trueFalse.statement: At least 10 dogs must be harnessed at all times during the race.
trueFalse.correction: A minimum of 5 dogs must be harnessed at all times during the race.

trueFalse.statement: The ceremonial start of the Iditarod Race begins in Willow.
trueFalse.correction: The ceremonial start is in Anchorage; the actual competitive race starts in Willow.

trueFalse.statement: Libby Riddles won the 1985 race after surviving a night on Norton Bay sea ice.
trueFalse.correction: Her brave decision to push through the storm created the 'Legend of Libby' and led to her victory.
